body:
You have seen it.

Someone opens a successful street food spot in Abuja, and before the weekend is over, three identical vendors spring up on the exact same street. We have over 270 fintechs trying to do the exact same thing—build another way for you to pay for plantain.

Nigeria has a massive copycat culture.

It is easy to blame the economy. Things are tight, and people are just trying to survive the structural gaps—no light, terrible networks, and shrinking purchasing power. When you see a commercial model working for someone else, the immediate instinct is to copy and paste.

But here is where it breaks down.

When you copy a business, you are only copying the output. You see the clean brand aesthetics and the customer queues. You do not see the founder's personal network. You do not see the backend partnerships, the supply chain systems, or the millions of Naira they lost trying to figure it out.

When you copy blindly without understanding the underlying commercial architecture, you will fail. And you will lose a lot of money doing it.

But a saturated market is not a death sentence. In fact, it is absolute proof of demand. With over 240 million people in Nigeria, one player cannot serve everyone. The market is hot.

The real challenge is figuring out how to differentiate when everyone is selling the exact same thing.

Sharon Kanu and I broke this down on this pisode of the Everything Entrepreneurship Podcast. We looked at why Nigerian founders keep falling into the copy-and-paste trap and the hidden costs of entering a crowded industry blindly.

More importantly, we discussed the one thing your competitors cannot reverse-engineer: your brand experience.

They can replicate your product. They can copy your pricing. But they cannot steal the trust and reliability you build with your customers.

If you are operating in a crowded market and trying to figure out how to stand out without just copying the next person, this conversation is for you.
summary: You come up with a business idea and realise five other people are already doing it. That feeling is where this episode starts. Seamas and Sharon are not here to lecture about market saturation, they are here to talk about something they have both seen, felt, and lived in the Nigerian business space. Why does it keep happening? Is it really our fault that we copy, or is something bigger going on? What actually happens when you enter a market with no competitive advantage? And is a saturated market even a death sentence in a country this size?  by the end of this episode you will have a clearer picture of the environment you are actually building in.
title: Why Is Every Business in Nigeria Doing the Same Thing? | Saturated Market Series Pt 1
